reports.name: Shohei Ohtani

The power contact is genuine: 93.4 mph average exit velocity and a 15.8% barrel rate combine with a walk rate that nearly touches the top of the league, and the projection of .281/.396/.539 with 37 home runs across 690 plate appearances reflects all of it translating at full workload. On the mound, 98.1 mph and 2486 rpm on the fastball underpin that xERA, and the 27.9% strikeout rate does the rest. The whole profile hinges on durability, and if he holds up as a starter and a near-everyday DH, the ceiling here isn't a range, it's a category of one.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: The contact quality is almost absurdly clean for a 22-year-old: 93.4 mph average exit velocity, 51.7% hard-hit rate, and a .374 xwOBA that the .282/.363/.552 projection treats as a foundation rather than a ceiling. He draws walks at 12.9% and strikes out at just 17.8%, which is a rare combination at this age and the whole reason the projection lands at 46 home runs across 692 plate appearances. The profile hinges on the discipline holding — if the chase rate creeps up as pitchers map his tendencies deeper into his career, the strikeout rate follows and the walk rate erodes, and you're left with a heavy-contact slugger who is still very good but no longer this good. The defense is a liability and the speed is negligible, so the entire bet is on the bat, and right now the bat is making that a comfortable bet.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA of .310 at the 100th percentile tells you the contact quality isn't a mirage — he's hitting the ball as hard as almost anyone, with a 93.2 mph average exit velocity and 52.8% hard-hit rate, and then adding 30.3 ft/s sprint speed that turns singles into doubles and doubles into triples before the stolen base total even gets going. The 32.8% chase rate is the one thing keeping this profile from being airtight; if pitchers find a way to exploit it consistently, the .291 projection slides and the whole value calculation tilts toward the speed. But ValuCast projects 47 steals alongside a .844 OPS, and that combination at shortstop, at 25, is about as clean a profile as this exercise produces.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact quality is historically clean: a .603 xSLG and 22.6% barrel rate that both sit at the absolute ceiling of the Statcast leaderboard, paired with a 16.5% walk rate that belongs in the same conversation. The one live wire is a 31.4% whiff rate, which means pitchers will keep hunting his bat — and if his swing-and-miss doesn't tighten, some of that xSLG stays theoretical. What makes the profile hold anyway is that he's not chasing to get there; a 22.8% chase rate is well below average, so the whiffs are coming on pitches he's actually offering at, not on junk out of the zone. If the strikeouts plateau rather than improve, he's a .894 OPS middle-of-the-order force; if he finds even modest contact gains, 37 home runs with a .382 OBP is a floor, not a ceiling.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The 49.6% hard-hit rate sits alongside a 36.4% chase rate, and that tension is the whole Crow-Armstrong profile in two numbers. He makes genuinely loud contact when he gets to his pitch, but he's hunting too often outside the zone, and the 25.4% strikeout rate is the tax. What saves the profile from contradiction is the .366 xwOBA, which says the quality of contact is outrunning the swing decisions right now, and 29.4 ft/s sprint speed that turns singles into doubles and steals into a real weapon. If the chase rate tightens even modestly, you get a .276/.356/.499 slash with 31 home runs and 39 steals, a genuine five-category force in the middle of a lineup; if it stays where it is, he's a volatile everyday player with loud stretches and long cold ones.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The contact hasn't caught up to the power yet, and it may never fully close — but at 23, Kurtz doesn't need it to. His 94.4 mph average exit velocity and 18.7% barrel rate sit at the very top of the league, and an 18.9% walk rate that leads all of baseball means pitchers who try to avoid the damage are just feeding a different problem. The 31.3% strikeout rate is the hinge: if he sharpens contact within the zone, the .386 xwOBA becomes a floor; if the 36.4% whiff rate proves sticky, he's a three-true-outcomes first baseman with elite upside rather than a true middle-of-the-order anchor. The projection calling for 37 home runs and a .400 OBP in a full season isn't a stretch given what the contact quality already shows, just waiting on a 23-year-old to figure out the last piece.

reports.name: Yordan Alvarez

The barrel rate sits at 19.3% and the walk rate at 15.1%, and together they explain how a hitter with ordinary sprint speed still projects to a 1.028 OPS: he doesn't need to beat out grounders because he almost never hits weak ones. The profile hinges on health, full stop — 674 projected plate appearances is the whole argument, and if he loses significant time the counting stats drop without changing what he is. What he is, when upright and in the lineup, is the most complete offensive player in the American League.

reports.peak_summary: Projection: mid-rotation starter or better with low risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 72.7 IP.
reports.published_report: A 1.4 ERA over 72.7 innings at Double-A isn't a hot month, it's a full argument. Kade Anderson has walked 10 batters all season, and when that translates to MLB context, his projected BB/9 of 2.1 sits more than a full walk below the league average; the strikeout rate translates to 10.0 K/9 against an MLB average of 8.6. Every skill grade in the profile comes back 80, miss, command, dominance, run prevention, so the question isn't whether the stuff is there but whether a 21-year-old left-hander can hold this shape against better hitters as he climbs. If he does, the ceiling is a mid-rotation starter or better, and the floor is a multi-inning arm who still beats most MLB rosters.

reports.name: Franklin Arias
reports.peak_summary: Projection: impact everyday bat with low risk. The current bat shape is impact over 299 PA.
reports.published_report: A 1.02 OPS at Double-A, at 20, with a 13% strikeout rate — that's not a guy surviving a level, that's a guy embarrassing it. Franklin Arias's translated walk rate beats the MLB average and his translated strikeout rate sits well below it, which means the bat-to-ball isn't just a Double-A illusion built on soft competition. The .270 ISO over 299 PA translates to .183 against big-league pitching, still above the MLB mean, so the power carries even after the level discount. If it holds at the next two levels, he's an impact everyday shortstop; if the strikeout rate bloats as velocity and spin get sharper, you're looking at a solid regular who probably slides off short, but a 70% projection for Regular-or-better on a 20-year-old with this contact shape is a number you don't talk yourself out of easily.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The contact quality is legitimate — 52.9% hard-hit rate puts him near the top of the league, and a .286 xBA suggests he's leaving hits on the table rather than collecting cheap ones. The tension in the profile is that a 28.6% whiff rate bleeds power out of the barrel: the xSLG sits at .433 while the xBA runs hot, meaning he makes loud contact when he connects but misses enough to suppress the home run total, which the projection caps at 17. What he is, fully assembled, is a .280 hitter with elite speed (29.0 ft/s, 36 projected steals) who generates hard contact at a near-elite rate but doesn't barrel balls often enough to turn that into a true power profile, the whole package projecting to a .772 OPS over a full season's workload. If the whiff rate tightens, the slugging catches up and the power numbers look conservative; if it doesn't, you're paying for a speed-and-contact profile from a name that still carries top-of-the-order expectations.

reports.name: Gunnar Henderson
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile on Henderson is quietly uncomfortable for a guy who finished top-three in AL MVP voting not long ago. His xwOBA sits at .307 and his xBA at .235, both in the bottom third of qualified hitters, and the exit-velocity story doesn't rescue it — 89.4 mph average exit velo lands exactly at the median. Where the profile holds up is contact quality in a different sense: his 43.8% hard-hit rate is genuinely above the crowd even if the barrel rate hasn't followed, and his 85th-percentile defense at shortstop means his floor is propped up by something that doesn't show in the slash line. The projection reads .239/.316/.430 with 28 home runs across 717 PA, which is a solid everyday shortstop if you weight the defense and the counting stats, but it's a comedown from the player Baltimore thought they had if the chase rate (32.2%) stays this loose and the barrel conversion doesn't climb.

At 22, with more upside penciled in than what's already on the page, this is one of the more compelling profiles in the Marlins system.

reports.name: Casey Schmitt
reports.published_report: The xBA at .293 and xSLG at .511 describe a contact quality profile that's genuinely elite, and the projection's .267/.304/.460 suggests he's been leaving real production on the table. The problem is obvious: a 2.1% walk rate is about as low as it goes in the majors, which is why a .356 xwOBA translates into a .304 OBP and why the projection's 26 home runs come with a runs total that doesn't match the power. Schmitt's profile hinges entirely on whether he can make enough contact at a high enough rate to survive without the walks, and with a 37.4% chase rate, the answer against quality pitching is often no. If he tightens the zone even modestly, there's a genuine above-average regular here; if not, he's a useful middle infielder whose counting stats will always feel a little thin relative to how hard he hits it.

At 11.6%, he's issuing free passes at a rate that poisons counts before his stuff can do its work, and an xERA of 4.33 reflects exactly that tension: elite swing-and-miss on one side, a bottom-fifth walk rate on the other. reports.name: Dustin May
reports.published_report: The fastball is legitimate, 96.9 mph with 2324 rpm spin, and the 6.8% walk rate is the cleanest thing on his card. Everything else tells you why a 3.85 xERA keeps getting buried under a 4.46 projected ERA: a 46.5% hard-hit rate that ranks near the bottom of the league, and a 22.0% whiff rate that doesn't generate enough swing-and-miss to neutralize the contact quality. He's keeping the ball in the park and limiting walks well enough to survive, but surviving isn't the same as pitching well, and the whole profile hinges on whether that hard-hit rate compresses as he settles into St. Louis. If it does, the xERA points toward a mid-rotation arm with real value across a full workload projected at 169.1 innings; if it doesn't, the 10 wins and 15 quality starts are about the ceiling.

reports.name: Taj Bradley
reports.published_report: The fastball grades out well at 96.9 mph with a strikeout rate of 26.9%, but the contact quality numbers are a genuine problem, and that tension defines everything about his ceiling. A 46.8% hard-hit rate and 91.8 mph average exit velo are the kind of numbers that don't coexist comfortably with a 3.96 xERA for very long. The walk rate at 10.0% is the other drag: the strikeouts don't come from chasing (28.8% chase rate sits well below average), so he's manufacturing Ks through whiffs in the zone while simultaneously putting too many runners on. If the walks tighten, he's a solid mid-rotation arm who misses enough bats to survive the hard contact; if they stay where they are, the projection's 3.99 ERA with a 1.3 WHIP over 160.8 innings is about the ceiling, not the floor.

reports.name: Bryce Elder
reports.published_report: The whole argument for Elder lives in the gap between his 3.61 xERA and a projected 4.22 ERA, and that gap is the story of a guy who gets hit on the barrel less often than nearly every starter in the league while striking out almost nobody. His 4.7% barrel rate is genuinely elite contact suppression, but a 20.0% strikeout rate means he needs to keep every softly-hit ball from finding a glove — there's no margin from the swing-and-miss side, where his 22.4% whiff rate sits well below average. The walk rate is quietly useful at 7.2%, keeping him from compounding trouble, and 176 projected innings say the stuff plays deep into games even if it doesn't overwhelm. He's a back-end starter who outperforms what hitters do to the ball, and if the barrel suppression softens even a tick, the strikeout profile doesn't bail him out.

reports.name: José Ramírez
reports.published_report: The contact and walk rates tell the real story here: a 17.3% whiff rate and 13.1% walk rate that both sit deep in the upper tier of the league, built on genuine zone discipline rather than passive hitting. Ramirez doesn't barrel the ball at an elite rate, 6.6%, but his xBA of .280 reflects how consistently he makes contact when he swings, and that contact quality supports the projected .343 OBP even as the raw power numbers cool from his peak. The projection of 18 home runs with 35 stolen bases across 513 plate appearances describes a player whose value has quietly shifted toward the legs and the walks, still a clear everyday third baseman but one whose fantasy ceiling now lives in run-scoring and steals rather than the middle-of-the-order thump he carried a few years back. If the sprint speed at 27.6 ft/s erodes, the stolen base number goes with it, and that's the one dependency that could quietly flatten an otherwise stable profile.

reports.name: Freddie Freeman
reports.published_report: The xwOBA of .391 and xBA of .295 aren't running ahead of his actual production — they're describing a hitter whose contact quality is genuinely elite even at 36. Freeman earns those numbers the disciplined way: 12.2% walks, 16.1% strikeouts, a chase rate that stays well below the league norm. The projection at .288/.377/.491 looks like a modest translation of that Statcast profile, and it probably is, given that sprint speed at 25.2 ft/s sits at the ninth percentile and any value left in his legs is purely incidental. If the contact and plate discipline hold at this level through a full season, he's a top-five first baseman; if age starts biting into the xSLG of .516, what remains is still a high-OBP regular who draws his walks and finds the barrel often enough to matter.

reports.name: Munetaka Murakami
reports.published_report: The tension here is almost comical: 99th-percentile exit velocity at 94.2 mph, a 20.7% barrel rate, a 17.9% walk rate, and then a 41.8% whiff rate sitting at the 1st percentile. Murakami hits the ball as hard as any hitter in this sample when he connects, and he walks at an elite clip, but he misses an enormous number of pitches — and that gap is what keeps a .379 xwOBA from translating into a batting average above his projected .234. The .517 projected SLG tells you the power is explosive enough to survive the strikeouts; 34 projected home runs from a first baseman who draws walks at that rate has genuine lineup value even with a 32.5% K rate dragging the average down. Everything hinges on whether MLB pitchers can continue to exploit the whiff rate or whether Murakami finds a zone, because at his contact floor he's an OBP-and-power corner bat, and at his ceiling he's something scarier.

reports.name: Colson Montgomery
reports.published_report: A 14.7% barrel rate with a 37.5% whiff rate is the whole contradiction in one profile. The power is genuinely there, sitting at the 90th percentile in barrels and projecting to 37 home runs over a full season, but contact is the load-bearing wall: a whiff rate in the 2nd percentile means those barrels come attached to a .221 AVG and a 31.5% strikeout rate that will test a rebuilding White Sox roster's patience. The xSLG of .461 lines up almost exactly with the projected .462 SLG, so the shape is consistent, but the .223 xBA tells you the contact problem isn't a bad-luck blip. If he can't tighten the zone enough to pull that whiff rate even toward league average, the floor is a pull-side slugger who bats seventh and strikes out at an alarming clip; if something clicks with bat-to-ball, the .766 OPS projection looks conservative for a shortstop who can barrel the ball at that rate.
